title: The Bed by the Window to the Wild Rumpus: Brooklyn, the Ridgefield House, and the Monsters Who Came on Sundays
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ellis Island, the parents cross
stops.date_confidence: Sadie Schindler arrives about 1911, Philip Sendak in 1914, naturalized 23 July 1929; the pin year defaults to the earlier crossing. Ellis Island as the specific port of entry is undocumented, and no manifest for either parent has been located.
stops.campa: Sadie Schindler comes over from Poland alone, and Philip Sendak follows her across a few years later, a dressmaker with a village behind him. Neither manifest has been found, so the inspection hall in the harbor stands in for a crossing whose paperwork is missing. What they carry through it is a country: the Yiddish of the Zambrow district, a trade, and a family that stays behind and writes letters. Philip will tell stories in that language at a bedside in Brooklyn for the next thirty years, and one of his listeners will draw them.
suggested_refs: Ellis Island passenger manifests for Sadie Schindler, c. 1911, and Philip Sendak, 1914, not yet located
sources: Selma G. Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak (1980)

stops.name: Bensonhurst, the birth of the third child
stops.date_confidence: attested; the street address of the birth is not recorded in any source consulted, and the pin is neighborhood-level
stops.campa: Maurice Bernard Sendak is born in the Bensonhurst section of Brooklyn to Philip and Sadie Sendak. Natalie is nine, Jack is five. The household speaks Yiddish, keeps the holidays the way the block keeps them, and moves whenever the rent goes up, so the family address is a sequence rather than a place. Twenty-four years earlier and eight miles north, Robert Oppenheimer was born on Riverside Drive into a German-Jewish immigrant house with paintings on the walls. The two boyhoods share a city and a century and nothing else.
suggested_refs: New York City birth register, Kings County, June 1928
sources: Selma G. Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak (1980)

stops.name: Bath Beach, the bed by the window
stops.date_confidence: the illnesses are attested in every biographical account and in Sendak's own interviews, but no source consulted fixes a year for any single one of them; measles, pneumonia and scarlet fever fall across the early 1930s and the date here is nominal
stops.campa: The boy is sick and stays sick: measles, pneumonia, scarlet fever, months of bed in a Brooklyn apartment while the other children are audible in the street below. He is given paper. He draws what he can see through glass and what his father supplies from the other side of the ocean, folk stories rebuilt each night out of a village that still exists. Reading and drawing are the two things a body confined to a mattress can do. He does both from the same year, and afterward he never does one without the other.
suggested_refs: Jonathan Cott's interviews with Sendak on the illnesses of early childhood
sources: Jonathan Cott, Sendak on Sendak interviews
Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak

stops.name: Highfields, the ladder at the nursery window
stops.date_confidence: the kidnapping is attested to 1 March 1932; Sendak is three, turning four that June, so accounts calling him four run a year early against the crime
stops.campa: A homemade ladder goes up against the second floor of a house in East Amwell Township and the Lindbergh baby is taken out of the nursery. Every radio in Brooklyn carries it for two months, and a three-year-old in Bensonhurst learns from it that a child can be lifted out of his own room while the house is awake downstairs. He never sees the place. Forty-nine years later he puts the ladder at Ida's window in Outside Over There and tells interviewers exactly where he got it.
suggested_refs: Highfields, the Lindbergh house near Hopewell, New Jersey, scene of the March 1932 kidnapping
sources: Sendak interviews with Jonathan Cott linking the case to Outside Over There

stops.name: Brooklyn, Fantasia at twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested to his twelfth year; the month, the day, and the theater are not recorded in the sources consulted, and the date defaults to January
stops.campa: Mickey Mouse has been in the house since he could hold a pencil, in the newspaper strips and on every licensed tin object a poor family can afford. At twelve he sits through Walt Disney's Fantasia and comes out having decided what he is: an illustrator, a maker of the drawn thing rather than a reader of it. He will keep the Disney fixation his whole life and defend it against people who think a serious artist should have outgrown a mouse. The mouse is later returned in full, naked and falling, in a kitchen made of milk bottles.
suggested_refs: Walt Disney, Fantasia (1940), the film Sendak credited with his vocation
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: Brooklyn, the news from Zambrow
stops.date_confidence: Sendak's own chronology dates his learning of the destruction of the family's Polish town to 1941; the killings themselves fall 1941 to 1943, the Jews of Zambrow being ghettoized and then deported to Treblinka and Auschwitz in the winter of 1942 to 1943. An earlier reading of this dossier gave 1940, which is wrong.
stops.campa: Word reaches the Brooklyn apartment that the town the letters came from is gone and the relatives with it. The Jews of Zambrow are ghettoized and then sent to Treblinka and Auschwitz. In Vienna the same machinery has already taken Sigmund Freud's four elderly sisters, who could not get exit papers when he got his. Sendak is thirteen. He will say for the rest of his life that the aunts and uncles who used to come on Sundays, loud and hungry and enormous over a child's head, are the faces he gave the Wild Things.
stops.quote: All children were in the Holocaust. Everybody was in the Holocaust.
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, PBS NOW with Bill Moyers, 12 March 2004, as reproduced on Wikiquote; the PBS transcript page was not retrievable for this dossier
suggested_refs: The deportation of the Jews of Zambrow to Treblinka and Auschwitz, winter 1942-43
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: Lafayette High School, the end of schooling
stops.date_confidence: the 1946 graduation is commonly reported but is not confirmed in the sources fetched for this dossier; the June month is assumed from ordinary commencement practice
stops.campa: He draws comic strips for the school paper at Lafayette High in Bensonhurst and does the work of a boy who has already chosen and is waiting out the requirement. There is no college in the plan and none in the family budget. He leaves with a portfolio rather than a transcript, which in the illustration trade of 1946 is the document that opens a door. The other boys go to the army or the garment district. He goes to Manhattan to paint backgrounds behind somebody else's characters.
suggested_refs: Lafayette High School yearbooks and student paper, Bensonhurst, 1942-1946
sources: Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak
standard Sendak biographical timeline, not confirmed in the fetched sources

stops.name: All-American Comics, backgrounds for Mutt and Jeff
stops.date_confidence: the job is dated 1946 to 1948 in standard biographical timelines, none of which names a document; the month is assumed
stops.campa: His first paid work in Manhattan is filling in what nobody looks at: the backgrounds behind Mutt and Jeff, drawn to somebody else's line, at somebody else's pace, for a syndicate that needs pages. He learns the discipline of the strip, which is the discipline of the picture book in miniature, one beat to a frame and the eye moved left to right without being told. He also learns that the comics he loved as a sick child were manufactured by men in a room, on a deadline. He holds the job for two years.
suggested_refs: All-American Comics syndicate records for the Mutt and Jeff strip, 1946-48
sources: standard Sendak biographical timeline; no document named in the sources consulted

stops.name: New York, Atomics for the Millions
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month of publication is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The professional career begins with a physics textbook. He illustrates Atomics for the Millions, an explanation of the atom for general readers published two years after Hiroshima, while Robert Oppenheimer is still being asked in public what he has done. Sendak is eighteen and drawing particles. It is the last job of his life in which the subject is handed to him whole by someone else, and the first line of a bibliography that will run to more than a hundred titles.
suggested_refs: Maxwell Leigh Eidinoff and Hyman Ruchlis, Atomics for the Millions (1947), illustrated by Sendak
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: FAO Schwarz, the windows on Fifth Avenue
stops.date_confidence: employment from 1948 is attested; the end year is given as 1951 by one lens of this dossier and 1952 by another, and the disagreement is not resolved here
stops.campa: He builds the windows at the FAO Schwarz toy store, staging small theatres of dolls and animals behind plate glass for people who are walking past on Fifth Avenue in winter coats. It is display work, and it is also, for four years, the closest thing to a stage he has. Passers-by stop; one of them is Ursula Nordstrom, who edits children's books at Harper and is looking at the windows rather than the toys. The introduction that follows takes him to Harper, which publishes his books for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: FAO Schwarz window displays, 745 Fifth Avenue, 1948-1952
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: Art Students League, the night classes
stops.date_confidence: the classes are attested; the start year is given as 1948 by one lens of this dossier and 1949 by another, a one-year disagreement left open
stops.campa: Days in the store window, evenings on West 57th Street at the Art Students League, painting and anatomy under John Groth. It is the only formal art training he ever gets, taken after work, in the room where a generation of American illustrators is taught to draw a body that can carry weight. He will insist afterward that he was self-taught, which is true of everything except the figure. The figure he learns here, and it is the reason Max's arms hold up when he is standing in a boat in a wolf suit.
suggested_refs: Art Students League of New York enrollment records, John Groth's evening class, 1948-1951
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: Harper offices, Ursula Nordstrom takes him on
stops.date_confidence: A Hole Is to Dig is attested to 1952 and The Wonderful Farm to 1951; the working relationship with Nordstrom has no single start date and the year here marks the book that made his name
stops.campa: Nordstrom gives him Marcel Ayme's The Wonderful Farm in 1951 and then Ruth Krauss's A Hole Is to Dig, and the small scratchy children in its margins make him, at twenty-four, an illustrator people ask for by name. The editorial partnership runs for decades out of these Manhattan offices, on paper, in letters he keeps. Uptown on Central Park West, Felix Adler's Ethical Culture School has been teaching children through fairy tales read as literature since the 1870s; no line runs from that classroom to this desk, and the two projects arrive at the same conviction anyway.
suggested_refs: Leonard S. Marcus, ed., Dear Genius: The Letters of Ursula Nordstrom (1998)
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

segments.name: Greenwich Village and the Wild Things

stops.name: Greenwich Village, Eugene Glynn
stops.date_confidence: the partnership is attested from 1957; no month is given, and the relationship is kept private for five decades and disclosed only in September 2008
stops.campa: He is twenty-eight and has just published Kenny's Window, his first book as his own author. In the same year he begins living with Eugene David Glynn, a psychoanalyst two years his elder who works with adolescents and writes about art. The arrangement lasts fifty years and is not spoken of outside the house. His parents are never told. Friends know; the reading public, the librarians, the schools that hand out his books by the thousand do not, and will not until he is eighty years old and Glynn is a year dead.
suggested_refs: Eugene David Glynn, Desperate Necessity: Writings on Art and Psychoanalysis (2008)
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: 29 West 9th Street, the wild things are drawn
stops.date_confidence: the address and the year of composition are attested; the months of writing and drawing are not documented
stops.campa: In a basement apartment on West 9th Street, a year after the four small volumes of the Nutshell Library, he writes a story of about three hundred and thirty-eight words and draws a boy sent to bed without supper. The monsters he gives the boy are the Sunday relatives of Bensonhurst: bulging eyes, bad teeth, hands that reach for a child's cheek and pinch it, voices saying they could eat him up. Max sails a year and a day, is made king, and comes home to find the supper still hot. The rumpus takes three double-page spreads and no words at all.
stops.quote: "And now," cried Max, "let the wild rumpus start!"
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, Where the Wild Things Are (Harper and Row, 1963), text as reproduced on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The basement apartment at 29 West 9th Street, Greenwich Village, where the book was made

stops.name: Harper and Row, the book is published
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 November 1963
stops.campa: Where the Wild Things Are goes out as a forty-page hardcover. Librarians write in to say it will frighten children; psychologists write in to say the same; Bruno Bettelheim attacks it without having read it. The children take it and keep it. By 2009 it has sold over nineteen million copies worldwide, about ten million of them in the United States, and has been translated into so many languages that no sourced count could be produced. Sendak is thirty-five and will be introduced by this one title for the remaining forty-nine years of his life.
stops.quote: Please don't go. We'll eat you up. We love you so.
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, Where the Wild Things Are (Harper and Row, 1963), text as reproduced on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: First printing, Where the Wild Things Are, Harper and Row, 13 November 1963

stops.name: Chicago, the Caldecott Medal
stops.date_confidence: the 1964 award is attested from the American Library Association winners archive; the ceremony date within the year is not established in the sources consulted and June is a default
stops.campa: The American Library Association gives the Caldecott Medal to the book its own members have been writing letters about, and the argument ends the way arguments about children's books end, with a gold seal on the jacket. He uses the acceptance speech to say what he will keep saying: that children survive their own terror daily and know more about it than the adults buying the book. From here he is not an illustrator who also writes. The label that follows him, preeminent American picture-book artist of the century, is fixed before he is forty.
suggested_refs: Sendak's 1964 Caldecott acceptance speech, reprinted in Caldecott and Co. (1988)
sources: American Library Association, Caldecott Medal winners archive

stops.name: Philadelphia, the first visit to the Rosenbach
stops.date_confidence: the first visit is attested to 1966; no month is given. The two lenses of this dossier disagree about the museum's coordinates by roughly 200 metres and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: He walks into a brownstone on Delancey Place that holds Melville's own copies and the manuscript of Ulysses, and finds the institution that will keep his working papers. Over the next decades he deposits thousands of original drawings there and it builds him a gallery, the largest single collection of his working process anywhere: pencil roughs, dummies, corrected proofs, the whole visible machinery behind books that look, on the shelf, like they arrived finished.
suggested_refs: The Maurice Sendak Gallery, Rosenbach Museum and Library, 2008-2010 Delancey Place, Philadelphia
sources: Rosenbach Museum and Library institutional history

stops.name: England, the heart attack at thirty-eight
stops.date_confidence: 1967 is attested from Sendak's own chronology; the English town is not named in any source consulted and the pin defaults to London, the month is not recorded
stops.campa: He is thirty-eight, working in England, when his heart stops behaving and he is put in a hospital bed for the first time since the Brooklyn apartment of his childhood. The sick child of 1930 returns bodily and stays: from this year forward he works against a known mortality, which he mentions in interviews with a bluntness that unsettles the interviewers. His mother is diagnosed with cancer the same year. The dog is at home in New York, old, and he is not there.
suggested_refs: Sendak's own chronology: 1967, heart attack in England, and the death of Jennie
sources: Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak

stops.name: Greenwich Village, Jennie dies
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested to 1967; no month is recorded and June is a default. An earlier reading of this dossier placed the death at Ridgefield, which is impossible: Sendak did not buy that house until 1972.
stops.campa: Jennie, the Sealyham terrier who has been in his books since the beginning, sitting in the corners of other people's stories, dies in the year of his heart attack. He answers by writing her a book in which she leaves home because there must be more to life than having everything, becomes leading lady of the World Mother Goose Theatre, and does not come back. Higglety Pigglety Pop! is published the same year. It is a children's book about a death, written by a man who has just been shown his own.
stops.quote: There must be more to life than having everything!
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, Higglety Pigglety Pop! (Harper and Row, 1967), text as reproduced on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Higglety Pigglety Pop! or There Must Be More to Life (Harper and Row, 1967)
sources: Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak

stops.name: Brooklyn, the parents die
stops.date_confidence: Sadie Sendak dies in 1968 per Sendak's own chronology, not 1967 as one lens of this dossier had it; she is diagnosed with cancer in 1967, which is the likely source of the conflation. Philip Sendak dies in 1970 [R], with no confirmed date or place. No cemetery is named in any source consulted, and this pin marks the family's Brooklyn streets rather than a grave.
stops.campa: Sadie Sendak dies in 1968, a year after the diagnosis. Philip follows in 1970. With them goes the generation that carried the village across the ocean, the Sunday voices, the folk material told at a sick boy's bedside in a language his own books will never print a word of. No reachable source names the ground either of them is buried in. The son who drew their relatives as monsters with yellow eyes spends the next four decades saying in public that everything he made came out of that apartment.
suggested_refs: Philip Sendak, In Grandpa's House, translated from the Yiddish and illustrated by Maurice Sendak (1985)
sources: Lanes, The Art of Maurice Sendak

stops.name: New York, In the Night Kitchen
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month given
stops.campa: Mickey falls out of his pajamas, out of his bed, and into a kitchen where three bakers with Oliver Hardy's face are making the morning cake. The skyline of that kitchen is built of milk bottles and flour sacks lettered like 1930s advertising, and readers who grew up near the boardwalk recognize Coney Island in it, as Sendak himself did. He draws the boy naked because the boy is naked. American libraries put the book on the most-challenged list, and librarians take pens to the pages and give the child a diaper.
suggested_refs: Library copies of In the Night Kitchen with the nudity inked over, 1970s
sources: American Library Association most-challenged books lists

stops.name: Bologna, the Hans Christian Andersen Medal
stops.date_confidence: the 1970 award is attested from the IBBY winners list; the host city of the ceremony is contradicted inside this dossier, one lens giving Bologna from standard award history and another flagging the city as unconfirmed. The pin defaults to Bologna and the month is unknown.
stops.campa: The International Board on Books for Young People gives him the Hans Christian Andersen Medal for illustration, and he is the first American to take it. Europe has been reading him in translation for seven years, in a book trade whose center of gravity in those decades is the fair at Bologna. The Caldecott had been an American jury on an American book. This one is judged across languages, and it goes to the man who draws monsters for five-year-olds in Brooklyn. He is forty-two and has been publishing for twenty-three years.
suggested_refs: IBBY Hans Christian Andersen Award, illustration medal, 1970
sources: IBBY Hans Christian Andersen Award winners list
Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: Ridgefield, the house in Fairfield County
stops.date_confidence: the 1972 move is attested from Britannica, the Maurice Sendak Foundation, and Sendak's own chronology; one lens of this dossier dated it 1985, which is thirteen years late and is discarded. The street address of the house is a gap.
stops.campa: He buys a converted farmhouse in Ridgefield, Connecticut, and moves out of Manhattan with Eugene Glynn, keeping a pied-a-terre at 40 Fifth Avenue for the work that requires a city. The property gets a studio, dogs, and eventually a small pet cemetery he tends himself. Thirty-nine years earlier, twenty-five miles down the same Fairfield County corridor, Buckminster Fuller was founding the Dymaxion Corporation at Bridgeport. Sendak spends the next forty years here, drawing at a table in the country, and dies twenty minutes up the road.
suggested_refs: The Sendak house and studio at Ridgefield, Connecticut, now the seat of the Maurice Sendak Foundation

stops.name: Weston, the Weston Woods films
stops.date_confidence: the collaboration is attested across the 1960s and 1970s; no single year is documented and 1973 is nominal
stops.campa: Morton Schindel's Weston Woods Studios, a few towns over, has been turning picture books into short films since the 1950s, moving the camera across the artist's own pages rather than reanimating them. Sendak works with the studio on adaptations including Where the Wild Things Are. The method suits him. Nothing is redrawn by another hand, and each picture holds the screen for the length of a sentence read aloud, which is the length he drew it for. It is the first time his images are given sound and a measured number of seconds to work in.
suggested_refs: Weston Woods Studios production files, Weston, Connecticut

stops.name: New York, Really Rosie with Carole King
stops.date_confidence: the year of the animated television special is attested; the broadcast date is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Rosie is a girl from a Brooklyn stoop who announces that she is the biggest star on her block and directs everybody else's part in the film of her life. Carole King writes the songs, Sendak writes the script and draws it, and the special goes out on American television. It is his first work made directly for the screen rather than adapted onto it afterward, songs and pictures built together from the start instead of one following the other, a stoop turned into a soundstage by a girl who never leaves the block.
suggested_refs: Really Rosie, animated television special, songs by Carole King, 1975
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: Ridgefield, Outside Over There
stops.date_confidence: the year of publication is attested; no month given
stops.campa: Ida is left minding the baby while her father is away at sea, and the goblins come in at the window by a ladder and take the child, leaving a thing made of ice in the cradle. He works on the book for years and calls it the hardest thing he has made. The ladder is the Lindbergh ladder, which he says outright. The girl left in charge of an infant is his sister Natalie, nine years older, who minded him. The palette is Mozart and German romantic painting, and the story underneath is a kidnapping he heard about on the radio at three.
suggested_refs: Outside Over There (Harper and Row, 1981), the third panel of the trilogy with Wild Things and Night Kitchen
sources: Sendak interviews on the Lindbergh case

stops.name: Manhattan, the National Book Award
stops.date_confidence: the 1982 award is attested from National Book Foundation records; the ceremony date is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Outside Over There takes the National Book Award, and the prize lands on the book of his that sells least and costs him most. Adults review it as though it were a novel, which is the reception he has been asking for since the 1960s and does not entirely enjoy when it arrives. He is fifty-three, has buried his parents, his dog, and his own confidence in his heart, and has just published the closest thing to an autobiography he will ever draw, with a nine-year-old girl standing in for him.
suggested_refs: National Book Foundation award records, Picture Books category, 1982

stops.name: Houston, The Magic Flute
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested from Houston Grand Opera production history; the premiere date within the season is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Houston Grand Opera asks him for sets and costumes for Mozart's The Magic Flute, and the illustrator who has been listening to Mozart at the drawing table since he was a young man is given the stage itself. He designs a serpent, a trial by fire, and a night sky for the Queen of the Night to sing under. The commission opens the second half of his working life. From here he is as often in a scene shop as at a drawing table, and a production takes him years where a book took him months.
suggested_refs: Houston Grand Opera, The Magic Flute, 1980, designs by Maurice Sendak

stops.name: Brussels, the premiere at La Monnaie
stops.date_confidence: attested to 28 November 1980. One lens of this dossier gave 25 November and another dated a vague stage adaptation to 1979, which is the year the collaboration began rather than the year of the premiere; both are discarded.
stops.campa: Oliver Knussen sets Where the Wild Things Are as an opera and Sendak writes the libretto out of his own three hundred words. It opens at the Theatre Royal de la Monnaie in Brussels under the French title Max et les Maximonstres, Ronald Zollman conducting, with Sendak's sets and costumes. The monsters are now sung, and the rumpus, which on the page took three wordless spreads, has to be scored. Knussen keeps revising the thing for years afterward, unsatisfied, in the way Sendak keeps redrawing a face until the eyes are wrong enough.
suggested_refs: Max et les Maximonstres, world premiere, Theatre Royal de la Monnaie, Brussels, 28 November 1980

stops.name: Seattle, the Nutcracker for Pacific Northwest Ballet
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the December premiere date of the production is not established in the sources consulted and January is a placeholder
stops.campa: Kent Stowell rechoreographs The Nutcracker for Pacific Northwest Ballet and Sendak designs it, pulling the ballet away from the Victorian sugar plum and back toward Hoffmann's harder story, with imagery out of his own books in the growing tree and the mouse king. The production runs in Seattle for decades and is filmed. A child can meet a Sendak drawing at Christmas this way, at ballet scale and moving, without knowing that the same hand drew the creatures the teacher reads out in spring.
suggested_refs: Pacific Northwest Ballet, Nutcracker, choreography Kent Stowell, designs Maurice Sendak, 1983
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, Maurice Sendak entry

stops.name: London, the final version at the National Theatre
stops.date_confidence: attested to 9 January 1984
stops.campa: Four years of revision after Brussels, Knussen's finished score is given at the National Theatre in London by Glyndebourne Touring Opera with the composer conducting. Whether the work's proper title in English is Where the Wild Things Are or the Brussels French Max et les Maximonstres is still argued in the reference literature and remains unsettled. What is settled is that a forty-page picture book from a Greenwich Village basement now exists as a repertory opera with a printed score.
suggested_refs: Glyndebourne Touring Opera at the National Theatre, London, 9 January 1984

stops.name: Glyndebourne, the double bill
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested from Glyndebourne archival production records; the month is not given and defaults to the summer festival season
stops.campa: Glyndebourne stages the two Knussen and Sendak operas together, Where the Wild Things Are and Higglety Pigglety Pop!, in the Sussex countryside, with Sendak designing both. The bill puts Max and Jennie the terrier on one evening's program: the boy who sails away and comes home to a hot supper, and the dog who leaves home because there must be more to life than having everything and never comes back. Knussen composed both, Sendak wrote both librettos, and the two stories divide one evening between them.
suggested_refs: Glyndebourne Festival Opera archival production records, 1984 Knussen and Sendak double bill
sources: Glyndebourne Festival Opera archival production records

stops.name: Princeton, the honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: the 1984 degree is attested; the commencement month is assumed. The coordinates are inherited byte-identical from einstein.journey.json, the atlas's canonical Princeton pin.
stops.campa: Princeton gives him a doctorate he did not go to college to earn, the first in a line of them that will run through the University of Connecticut and Goucher. Albert Einstein came into New York Harbor by tugboat in October 1933 to avoid the crowds on the pier and settled in this town for the rest of his life. Sendak arrives for an afternoon, in a rented gown, to be told by an institution that the drawings are scholarship. He collects the honors carefully and remains, in interviews, a man with an eighth-grade opinion of universities.
suggested_refs: Princeton University honorary degree citations, 1984

stops.name: Ridgefield, We Are All in the Dumps with Jack and Guy
stops.date_confidence: the year of publication is attested; no month given. The quote at this stop is dated 20 September 1993 to a New York Times interview whose page is not directly fetchable from this environment.
stops.campa: He takes two nursery rhymes and builds them into a book about children sleeping under cardboard in a city, about AIDS, about a baby stolen by rats and a moon that turns into a cat. Newspapers report it as a departure. It is not a departure; it is the Sunday relatives and the ladder and the boy in the pot, arrived at the decade that gave him the words for them. He is sixty-five, has been called controversial since 1965, and has stopped bothering to say that a child's fear is not something an adult invented for the child.
stops.quote: I have this idiot name tag which says "controversial." I've had it since 1965, with "Where the Wild Things Are."
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, 'Maurice Sendak Sheds Moonlight on a Dark Tale,' The New York Times, 20 September 1993; page not directly fetchable, confirmed through search-result text and quotation databases
suggested_refs: We Are All in the Dumps with Jack and Guy (HarperCollins, 1993)
sources: The New York Times, 20 September 1993, cited secondhand

stops.name: The White House, the National Medal of Arts
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 September 1996 from National Endowment for the Arts recipient records
stops.campa: President Clinton hangs the National Medal of Arts on a man whose entire body of work is forty pages at a time and is read chiefly by people under seven. The citation is for American illustration and children's literature. Twelve years later a president will read his book aloud on the South Lawn at an Easter Egg Roll, doing the voices, and the Postal Service will put the Wild Things on a stamp. The republic has decided that its monsters are national property, which is a conclusion Sendak accepts without pretending to have aimed at it.
suggested_refs: National Endowment for the Arts, National Medal of Arts recipients, 1996
sources: National Endowment for the Arts recipient records, 1996

stops.name: Stockholm, the first Astrid Lindgren Memorial Award
stops.date_confidence: the 2003 award is attested; the ceremony date and venue are a gap in the sources consulted, and the pin is city-level for the Swedish body that administers the prize
stops.campa: Sweden establishes the world's largest prize for children's literature in memory of Astrid Lindgren and gives the first one to Sendak, jointly with the Austrian writer Christine Nostlinger. Lindgren wrote a girl who lifts a horse and lives without parents; Sendak drew a boy who sails to where the monsters are and sails back for supper. The award is worth five million kronor and is administered from Stockholm. He is seventy-four and by now collects such things the way other men collect the mail.

stops.name: Ridgefield, Brundibar with Tony Kushner
stops.date_confidence: the 2003 publication is attested; no month is given in the sources consulted and June is a placeholder
stops.campa: Tony Kushner adapts Brundibar, the children's opera performed fifty-five times by Jewish children imprisoned at Theresienstadt before the transports took the cast to Auschwitz, and Sendak illustrates it. He is seventy-five and has spent his whole career being told his books are too dark for children. Here the children in the pictures are the ones who were murdered, and the bully with the mustache is drawn as what he was. The material he has worked around since the news from Zambrow in 1941 is finally on the page directly.
stops.quote: When you hide another story in a story, that's the story I am telling the children.
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, interview, 'Sendak on Sendak,' Rosenbach Museum and Library, Philadelphia, 2007/2008, as reproduced on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Tony Kushner and Maurice Sendak, Brundibar (Hyperion, 2003)

stops.name: Ridgefield, Eugene Glynn dies
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested to 15 May 2007; the place is given as Sendak's residence and is approximate
stops.campa: Glynn dies after fifty years, having lived most of them in this house with a man the reading public believed to be a bachelor recluse. Sendak gives one million dollars to the Jewish Board of Family and Children's Services in his memory, the agency where Glynn worked with adolescents. He is seventy-eight, alone in a farmhouse with the dogs and the pet cemetery, and there is no one left alive who was told about the arrangement at the time it began.
stops.quote: Art has always been my salvation.
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, PBS NOW with Bill Moyers, 12 March 2004, three years before Glynn's death, as reproduced on Wikiquote; the PBS transcript page was not retrievable for this dossier

stops.name: New York, the interview with Patricia Cohen
stops.date_confidence: published 9 to 10 September 2008. One lens of this dossier credited Terry Gross, conflating this with her NPR Fresh Air conversation of 2011, a different occasion, and another said the disclosure came after his death, which is wrong by nearly four years.
stops.campa: Patricia Cohen of The New York Times sits with him in Ridgefield for a piece headed Concerns Beyond Just Where the Wild Things Are, and he tells her he is gay and that Eugene Glynn was his partner for fifty years. He is eighty. He says he never told his parents, and that a gay man who made his living from children's books in 1957 did not tell anyone. The sentence goes around the world in a day. The books stay exactly what they were, and the schools keep handing them out.

stops.name: Ridgefield, Bumble-Ardy and the last interview
stops.date_confidence: Bumble-Ardy is attested to 2011 and the Fresh Air conversation to September 2011; the recording date within the month is not given
stops.campa: Bumble-Ardy is a pig who throws himself a ninth birthday party after his parents are eaten, and it is the last book published in Sendak's lifetime. He made it, he says, while sitting with a dying Eugene Glynn. In September he talks to Terry Gross on NPR for what turns out to be the final recorded interview of his life, and closes it by wishing her well and telling her to live. He is eighty-three, is not pretending to be anything other than near the end, and sounds happier about the arrangement than she does.
stops.quote: I wish you all good things. Live your life, live your life, live your life.
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, interview with Terry Gross, NPR Fresh Air, September 2011, quoted verbatim in Maria Popova, The Marginalian, 3 January 2013

stops.name: Danbury Hospital, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 May 2012, four days after a stroke. Two lenses of this dossier gave two different and both incorrect coordinate pairs for the hospital; the value here is 24 Hospital Avenue, Danbury.
stops.campa: He has a stroke and dies four days later at Danbury Hospital, aged eighty-three. Fifty-five years earlier, on the other side of this same Connecticut town, Wilhelm Reich walked through the gate of the federal penitentiary to serve a sentence he did not survive. Danbury holds both of them, a prison and a hospital and no connection between the two men except a name on a map. Sendak dies twenty minutes from the farmhouse, in the county he moved to in 1972 to get away from the city he could never quite stop drawing.
stops.quote: It is a blessing to get old. It is a blessing to find the time to do the things, to read the books, to listen to the music.
stops.quote_source: Maurice Sendak, interview with Terry Gross, NPR Fresh Air, September 2011, eight months before his death, quoted verbatim in Maria Popova, The Marginalian, 3 January 2013
suggested_refs: Danbury Hospital, 24 Hospital Avenue, Danbury, Connecticut

stops.name: Ridgefield, the ashes
stops.date_confidence: the cremation and the absence of any public grave are attested; the scattering site is undisclosed in every source consulted, the Ridgefield property is tradition only, and the date is a placeholder in the days after the death
stops.campa: By his own arrangement he is cremated and the ashes are scattered somewhere nobody has published. There is no stone, no plot, no address for anyone who wants to visit. The assumption among those who write about him is that they went into the ground of the Ridgefield property, near the pet cemetery he dug and tended himself for forty years, but no consulted source confirms it. The man who spent his career drawing what happens to children who are taken away leaves no place to be taken to.
suggested_refs: The Maurice Sendak Foundation, Ridgefield, Connecticut, established at the house

stops.name: New York, My Brother's Book
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 2013; the day of publication is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The posthumous book is for Jack, the brother who died in 1995, and it is watercolor and Blake and Shakespeare's Winter's Tale, two boys separated by a falling star. It is the closest he ever comes to the illuminated page, and it is published nine months after his death. The same year Spike Jonze, who filmed Where the Wild Things Are in live action in 2009 with Sendak's blessing, dedicates Her to his memory, and New York puts him in its Writers Hall of Fame with the novelists.

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Rosenbach and the estate
stops.date_confidence: the suit is attested to 2014 and the ruling to 2016; neither month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The museum that housed thousands of his drawings for four decades sues his estate over rare books he had promised it, including Melville and Blake he bought as a collector. In 2016 a Connecticut probate judge awards most of the disputed collection to the estate, and the Sendak material at Delancey Place thins out. Anyone searching the Rosenbach's own website afterward finds less about him than the secondary literature implies, and the reason is a docket rather than an absence of history.

stops.name: Denver, Wild Things Are Happening
stops.date_confidence: the Denver Art Museum run is attested to 2 October 2022 through 12 February 2023, correcting an earlier reading of this dossier that gave 2024-2025. One contradiction is left open: the same corrected note gives a Columbus Museum of Art opening of 20 October 2022, which overlaps the Denver run rather than preceding it, so the tour's order is unsettled.
stops.campa: The touring retrospective assembled with the Maurice Sendak Foundation, Wild Things Are Happening: The Art of Maurice Sendak, hangs the dummies, the pencil roughs, the opera designs, and the finished plates on museum walls. Denver takes it through the winter of 2023, and in April 2024 it opens at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles, a Jewish institution showing the Brundibar drawings alongside Max in his wolf suit. The dummies and the roughs were working paper. On these walls they are framed and lit like paintings.
